questions.title: Genitofemoral nerve injury during radical nephroureterectomy
questions.question: A patient with renal cell carcinoma undergoes radical nephroureterectomy with ligation of the renal artery, renal vein, and ureter. Which structure is most likely to be injured during the ureteric part of the procedure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Psoas major is the large muscle the genitofemoral nerve and ureter both travel across; it is a landmark for the dissection, not the structure typically injured.
explanations.B: Correct. The genitofemoral nerve runs on the anterior surface of psoas major, in close proximity to the gonadal vessels, ureter, and lower pole of the kidney, making it the structure most at risk when the renal vessels and ureter are mobilized and ligated for radical nephroureterectomy. Injury produces sensory loss over the anterior scrotum/labia and upper thigh (genital and femoral branches) and, in males, loss of the cremasteric reflex. Surgeons dissecting along psoas major during ureterolysis or gonadal vessel ligation are specifically taught to identify and preserve this nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The gonadal veins run parallel to the ureter and can be ligated deliberately as part of the procedure, but they are vessels, not the nerve most at risk of inadvertent injury described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava lies medial to the right kidney and is a major structure to protect during caval-side dissection, but it is not the structure classically injured during ureteric mobilization on either side.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sympathetic trunk lies more medially along the vertebral bodies, well away from the lateral retroperitoneal plane where the ureter and renal vessels are typically ligated.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that the genitofemoral nerve is the structure most at risk during ligation for radical nephroureterectomy.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Anatomy > Retroperitoneal relations of the kidney and ureter

questions.title: Acute interstitial nephritis from antibiotic hypersensitivity
questions.question: A patient develops fever, a maculopapular rash, and eosinophilia with red and white cells in the urine within about 3 days of starting a new antibiotic. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?

options.A: Acute interstitial nephritis due to a hypersensitivity reaction to the antibiotic

explanations.A: Correct. Acute interstitial nephritis caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to a drug, classically an antibiotic such as a penicillin, characteristically presents with peripheral and urinary eosinophilia, fever, and a maculopapular rash arising within days of exposure, together with hematuria and pyuria from interstitial inflammation. This drug-hypersensitivity pattern, with its rapid onset relative to a new drug and its allergic features, is the classic teaching vignette for AIN and is distinguished from other causes of acute kidney injury by exactly these features.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ischemic acute tubular necrosis follows a hypotensive or nephrotoxic insult and produces muddy-brown granular casts, not eosinophilia, fever, or a rash.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis follows a streptococcal infection by 1-3 weeks and presents with a nephritic picture (hematuria, hypertension, edema), not the eosinophilia-plus-rash pattern of a drug hypersensitivity reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy classically flares with gross hematuria concurrent with (not days after) a mucosal infection, and does not produce eosinophilia or a rash.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that antibiotic-induced acute interstitial nephritis presents with eosinophilia, fever, and a maculopapular rash within days of drug exposure.

questions.title: Macula densa basal Golgi apparatus
questions.question: On electron microscopy, macula densa cells of the distal tubule characteristically show which ultrastructural feature, reflecting their sensory/paracrine rather than absorptive function?

options.A: An apically located Golgi apparatus, as in typical absorptive tubular epithelium
options.C: Numerous apical microvilli forming a prominent brush border
options.D: Abundant basal infoldings with interdigitating mitochondria, as in principal cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. An apical Golgi is the arrangement seen in typical absorptive tubular epithelium (e.g., proximal tubule), not in the macula densa, which shows the reverse.
explanations.B: Correct. Macula densa cells show a reversed polarity compared with most tubular epithelium, with the Golgi apparatus located basally, facing the extraglomerular mesangium and juxtaglomerular apparatus, consistent with their role sensing luminal sodium chloride and signalling paracrine mediators toward the JGA rather than absorbing filtrate. This basal Golgi location is a distinctive, frequently tested exception to the usual apical-Golgi pattern of tubular cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A prominent apical brush border of microvilli is characteristic of the proximal convoluted tubule, which maximizes surface area for bulk reabsorption, not the macula densa.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extensive basal infoldings with interdigitating mitochondria are characteristic of principal cells of the collecting duct (an ion-transporting, energy-intensive epithelium), not the sensory macula densa.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that macula densa cells characteristically show a basally located Golgi apparatus on electron microscopy.

questions.title: Tram-track splitting in type 1 MPGN
questions.question: Which glomerular lesion is characterized by tram-track (double-contour) splitting of the glomerular basement membrane with subendothelial immune-complex deposits?

explanations.A: Correct. Type 1 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis shows mesangial and endocapillary proliferation with mesangial cell interposition between the endothelium and basement membrane, producing the classic "tram-track" double-contour appearance of the GBM on light and electron microscopy, together with subendothelial immune-complex deposits. It is a well-recognized cause of both nephrotic-range proteinuria and hypocomplementemia and is a frequently tested histologic pattern for exactly this reason.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial (not subendothelial) deposits producing a "spike-and-dome" appearance on silver stain, without tram-track splitting.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Minimal change disease shows normal glomeruli by light microscopy with only diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy; there is no basement membrane splitting or immune deposits.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis shows segmental scarring of some glomeruli, not diffuse tram-track GBM splitting.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that type 1 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis shows tram-track GBM splitting with subendothelial deposits.

questions.title: Afferent arteriolar dilatation increases renal blood flow
questions.question: Dilatation of the afferent arteriole, at constant efferent arteriolar tone, produces which effect on renal blood flow?

options.C: No change in renal blood flow, only in GFR
options.D: Decreases renal blood flow but increases GFR

explanations.A: Correct. Dilatation of the afferent arteriole lowers preglomerular resistance, which raises glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and increases both renal plasma flow and, at constant efferent tone, glomerular filtration rate. This is why physiologic states that dilate the afferent arteriole (such as prostaglandin-mediated autoregulation, or NSAIDs blocking that dilatation) directly affect renal blood flow, not just GFR.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Afferent arteriolar constriction, not dilatation, is what reduces renal blood flow by raising preglomerular resistance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Afferent arteriolar tone affects total renal vascular resistance directly, so renal blood flow changes together with GFR, not independently of it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes the effect of efferent arteriolar constriction (GFR rises while RBF may fall at higher degrees of constriction), the opposite scenario from afferent dilatation.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that afferent arteriolar dilatation increases renal blood flow.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Physiology > Renal vascular resistance and GFR regulation

questions.title: Sodium bicarbonate can cause hypokalemia
questions.question: A recognized adverse effect of sodium bicarbonate administration is which electrolyte disturbance?

options.D: Hypernatremia only, with no effect on potassium

explanations.A: Correct. Sodium bicarbonate raises extracellular pH, and the resulting alkalosis drives potassium into cells in exchange for hydrogen ions leaving the intracellular compartment, lowering serum potassium. This intracellular shift is a recognized adverse effect of bicarbonate therapy and is, in fact, exploited therapeutically as one of the shift-based treatments for hyperkalemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is caused by acidosis (the opposite process, hydrogen ions moving into cells and potassium moving out), not by bicarbonate-induced alkalosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate does not characteristically cause hypercalcemia; its major relevant electrolyte effect is the potassium shift described.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate does have a well-recognized effect on potassium (causing hypokalemia via the alkalosis-driven intracellular shift), so this option is incomplete/incorrect.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that sodium bicarbonate therapy can cause hypokalemia by driving potassium intracellularly.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Pharmacology > Sodium bicarbonate adverse effects

questions.title: Safe correction ceiling for severe hyponatremia
questions.question: A patient presents with a serum sodium of 116 mEq/L. To avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome, to what level should the serum sodium safely be raised within the first 24 hours of correction?

options.A: No more than about 124-126 mEq/L (a rise of about 8-10 mEq/L)
options.B: All the way to a normal value of about 140 mEq/L
options.C: No more than about 118 mEq/L (a rise of about 2 mEq/L)
options.D: It should be lowered further before any correction is attempted

explanations.A: Correct. To avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome, correction of severe or chronic hyponatremia is limited to a rise in serum sodium of no more than about 8-10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours, so a patient starting at 116 mEq/L should not be raised above roughly 124-126 mEq/L within the first day. This rate-limited approach is standard teaching precisely because overly rapid correction, not the hyponatremia itself, is what precipitates central pontine/extrapontine myelinolysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Correcting all the way to a normal serum sodium within 24 hours substantially exceeds the safe rate ceiling and risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A rise of only about 2 mEq/L is overly conservative relative to the accepted 8-10 mEq/L/24h ceiling and would undertreat a genuinely severe, symptomatic hyponatremia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Severe hyponatremia should be corrected, not further lowered; the teaching point concerns the rate and ceiling of correction, not withholding it.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that correction of severe hyponatremia is limited to about 8-10 mEq/L in the first 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Physiology > Sodium and water balance, correction limits

questions.title: Segmental necrosis and crescents in anti-GBM disease
questions.question: Which glomerular histologic finding — segmental fibrinoid necrosis with parietal epithelial cell proliferation — is characteristic of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease?

options.B: Diffuse mesangial IgA deposition without necrosis
options.C: Uniform thickening of the GBM without proliferation

explanations.A: Correct. Anti-GBM disease is a rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis in which glomeruli show segmental fibrinoid necrosis with parietal epithelial cell proliferation forming crescents, driven by linear IgG (and often C3) deposition along the GBM on immunofluorescence. This necrotizing, crescentic pattern accounts for the disease's rapid clinical deterioration and is a defining histologic feature taught alongside the linear immunofluorescence pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diffuse mesangial IgA deposition without necrosis describes IgA nephropathy, a distinct and generally more indolent glomerulopathy, not anti-GBM disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uniform GBM thickening without proliferation is the pattern of membranous nephropathy, not the necrotizing, crescentic pattern of anti-GBM disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Isolated foot process effacement without proliferative or necrotizing change is the pattern of minimal change disease, not anti-GBM disease.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that anti-GBM disease characteristically shows segmental glomerular necrosis with crescent formation.

questions.title: E. coli causes 90% of uncomplicated UTIs
questions.question: In a patient with a structurally and functionally normal (anatomically unremarkable) urinary tract, which organism causes approximately 90% of uncomplicated urinary tract infections?

explanations.A: Correct. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli accounts for approximately 90% of uncomplicated urinary tract infections in patients with a normal urinary tract, far more than any other single organism, owing to its adhesins (type 1 and P fimbriae) that allow it to colonize the periurethral area and ascend into the bladder. This dominance is why empiric therapy for uncomplicated cystitis is chosen to reliably cover E. coli.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is the second most common cause of uncomplicated UTI, particularly in young sexually active women, but accounts for a much smaller share than E. coli.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proteus mirabilis is more typical of complicated or catheter-associated UTIs and stone-forming (struvite) infections, not the dominant organism in uncomplicated, anatomically normal-tract UTIs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enterococcus faecalis is more characteristic of complicated, healthcare-associated, or catheter-related UTIs, not the leading cause of uncomplicated UTI in a normal urinary tract.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that E. coli causes about 90% of uncomplicated UTIs in patients with a normal urinary tract.

questions.title: Secondary amyloid nephropathy from chronic bronchiectasis
questions.question: A patient with longstanding chronic bronchiectasis develops heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema (a nephrotic syndrome picture). Which renal complication and mechanism best explain this?

options.A: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis from chronic suppurative inflammation
options.B: Primary (AL) amyloidosis from a plasma cell dyscrasia
options.D: Minimal change disease unrelated to the lung disease

explanations.A: Correct. Secondary (AA) amyloidosis is driven by chronic elevation of the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A in states of prolonged inflammation such as chronic bronchiectasis, chronic osteomyelitis, or rheumatoid arthritis; the AA protein deposits in the kidney and characteristically presents with a nephrotic syndrome picture. This link between a chronic suppurative source and secondary renal amyloidosis is a classic clinical vignette precisely because the two conditions are causally connected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary (AL) amyloidosis arises from a plasma cell dyscrasia producing immunoglobulin light chains, not from chronic infective/inflammatory lung disease; it would not be specifically linked to bronchiectasis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetic nephropathy requires a history of diabetes mellitus, which is not part of this vignette, and is not caused by chronic bronchiectasis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vignette specifically links a chronic suppurative condition to a secondary amyloid mechanism; calling the two "unrelated" ignores the well-established AA-amyloidosis pathway.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that secondary (AA) amyloidosis from chronic suppurative lung disease such as bronchiectasis can present as nephrotic syndrome.

questions.title: Sympathetic activity stimulates renin secretion
questions.question: Increased renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells can be produced by increased activity of which pathway, acting through beta-1 adrenergic receptors?

options.D: Renal sensory afferent activity alone, with no efferent component

explanations.A: Correct. Increased renal sympathetic nerve activity stimulates renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells directly via beta-1 adrenergic receptors. This is one of the three classic stimuli for renin release, alongside reduced afferent arteriolar (renal perfusion) pressure sensed by the intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism and reduced sodium chloride delivery sensed by the macula densa.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Parasympathetic (vagal) innervation is not a recognized stimulus for renin secretion; renin release is driven by sympathetic, not parasympathetic, tone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Somatic motor nerves innervate skeletal muscle and have no role in regulating juxtaglomerular cell renin release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pathway relevant to renin release from sympathetic stimulation is an efferent (motor) sympathetic pathway acting on beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells, not an isolated sensory afferent signal.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that increased renal sympathetic activity stimulates renin secretion via beta-1 adrenergic receptors.

questions.title: Glutamate decarboxylase is not a gamma-glutamyl cycle enzyme
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the enzymes of the gamma-glutamyl cycle (the glutathione-dependent transmembrane amino acid transport pathway)?

explanations.A: Correct. Glutamate decarboxylase converts glutamate to GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and plays no role in transmembrane amino acid transport; it is not one of the gamma-glutamyl cycle's enzymes. The gamma-glutamyl cycle, which transports amino acids across cell membranes (notably in the renal tubule and intestinal epithelium) using glutathione, is instead carried out by gamma-glutamyl transferase, gamma-glutamyl cyclotransferase, 5-oxoprolinase, gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase, and glutathione synthetase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gamma-glutamyl transferase, which transfers the gamma-glutamyl group of glutathione onto an amino acid at the cell membrane, is the first and defining step of the gamma-glutamyl cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gamma-glutamyl cyclotransferase, which converts the gamma-glutamyl-amino acid back into the free amino acid plus 5-oxoproline intracellularly, is a genuine gamma-glutamyl-cycle enzyme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glutathione synthetase, which regenerates glutathione from its constituent amino acids to complete the cycle, is a genuine gamma-glutamyl-cycle enzyme.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that glutamate decarboxylase is not an enzyme of the gamma-glutamyl cycle, distinguishing it from the cycle's true five enzymes.

questions.title: Congenital polycystic kidney disease from failed tubule union
questions.question: One proposed embryological mechanism for congenital (infantile-type) polycystic kidney disease is failure of normal union between which two tubule populations?

options.A: The ureteric-bud-derived collecting tubules and the metanephric excretory (nephrogenic) tubules
options.C: The proximal and distal convoluted tubules of the same nephron
options.D: The afferent and efferent arterioles of the glomerulus

explanations.A: Correct. One proposed embryological mechanism for congenital polycystic kidney disease is failure of normal union between the ureteric-bud-derived collecting tubules and the metanephric-mesenchyme-derived excretory (nephrogenic) tubules, so that fluid produced by the nephron cannot drain and the obstructed tubule dilates into a cyst. This failure-of-union mechanism is the classic embryological explanation taught for the congenital/infantile form of polycystic kidney disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesonephric and paramesonephric ducts give rise to the internal genital tract structures, not the collecting-duct/nephron drainage system implicated in polycystic kidney disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The proximal and distal convoluted tubules of a single nephron are already continuous by definition within one developing nephron; their relationship is not the failure-of-union mechanism described for cystic disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The afferent and efferent arterioles are vascular structures of the glomerular apparatus, unrelated to the tubular drainage failure implicated in polycystic kidney disease.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that failure of union between the collecting tubules and the excretory tubules is a proposed embryological cause of congenital polycystic kidney disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Embryology > Nephron and collecting-system development, cystic disease

questions.title: Check renal function before bisphosphonate for severe hypercalcemia
questions.question: Before starting intravenous bisphosphonate treatment for severe hypercalcemia, which baseline test should be obtained?

explanations.A: Correct. Intravenous bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid or pamidronate are renally excreted and can themselves cause nephrotoxicity, so a kidney function test should be obtained before starting bisphosphonate treatment for severe hypercalcemia, with doses adjusted or withheld for significant renal impairment. This baseline check is standard practice specifically because renal clearance determines both dosing and the risk of further renal injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates are cleared renally, not hepatically, so liver function testing is not the specific baseline check indicated before their use.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thyroid function is not the relevant baseline parameter for bisphosphonate safety; it is not affected by or a determinant of bisphosphonate clearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bisphosphonates do not require a baseline coagulation profile; their key safety concern is renal, not hemostatic.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that renal function must be checked before starting bisphosphonate treatment for severe hypercalcemia because bisphosphonates are renally excreted and potentially nephrotoxic.

questions.title: Mesangial cells and GBM turnover
questions.question: Which function of glomerular mesangial cells relates to the recycling of the glomerular basement membrane?

options.A: Phagocytic turnover of glomerular basement membrane material
options.B: Production of surfactant to reduce filtration surface tension
options.C: Secretion of erythropoietin in response to hypoxia

explanations.A: Correct. In addition to providing structural support for the glomerular capillary tuft and having contractile properties that help regulate glomerular capillary surface area, mesangial cells are phagocytic and contribute to turnover of the glomerular basement membrane, taking up and recycling GBM material and trapped macromolecules. This phagocytic/GBM-turnover role is a distinct, commonly tested function alongside their structural and contractile roles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Surfactant production is a function of type II pneumocytes in the lung, not glomerular mesangial cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Erythropoietin is produced by renal peritubular interstitial (fibroblast-like) cells in response to hypoxia, not by mesangial cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin D-binding protein is synthesized by the liver, not by mesangial cells; mesangial cells are not part of vitamin D handling.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that mesangial cells contribute to phagocytic turnover of the glomerular basement membrane.

questions.title: Small fraction of filtered water reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct
questions.question: Approximately what fraction of filtered water is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct, the final and most tightly ADH-regulated tubular segment?

options.D: Essentially 0%, since water reabsorption ends at the distal tubule

explanations.A: Correct. Of the water filtered at the glomerulus, roughly 65% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, about 15% in the descending thin limb of the loop of Henle, and up to about 10-15% more in the distal tubule and cortical collecting duct under maximal ADH; only a small remaining fraction, about 4-5%, is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct. Although numerically small, this last segment is the most tightly ADH-regulated and physiologically decisive for setting final urine osmolality.
explanations.B: Incorrect. About 65% of filtered water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, not the medullary collecting duct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No single nephron segment reabsorbs about 25% of filtered water under normal conditions in the standard teaching breakdown; this overstates the medullary collecting duct's numerical share.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Water reabsorption does not end at the distal tubule; the medullary collecting duct, under ADH control, reabsorbs a further small but physiologically critical fraction of filtered water.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that only about 4-5% of filtered water is reabsorbed in the medullary collecting duct.
questions.module_subject: ASU-UG > Physiology > Segmental renal handling of water

questions.title: Smooth yellow uric acid stones in gout
questions.question: A patient with gout forms a smooth, yellow renal stone that has enlarged into a branching (staghorn) configuration filling the renal pelvis and calyces. What is the composition of this stone?

explanations.A: Correct. Renal stones composed of uric acid form in the setting of persistently acidic, uric-acid-supersaturated urine, such as occurs in gout, and are classically smooth-surfaced and yellow (in contrast to the rough, spiculated appearance of calcium oxalate stones). Like struvite stones, pure uric acid stones can enlarge to fill the renal pelvis and calyces in a branching "staghorn" configuration, a point commonly missed by the oversimplified teaching that staghorn calculi are always struvite.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Calcium oxalate stones classically have a rough, spiculated, dark surface, not the smooth yellow appearance described, and are not specifically linked to gout.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While struvite stones are the classic cause of a staghorn calculus and form in chronically infected, alkaline urine, they are not specifically associated with gout and do not have the smooth yellow gross appearance described here, which points to uric acid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cystine stones occur in cystinuria, an inborn error of renal tubular amino acid transport, and are not linked to gout or to this smooth yellow gross appearance.
